content: Anthrax is a bacterial zoonotic disease that can occasionally infect humans and has the potential to be fatal. Vaccines developed to prevent anthrax include a live-attenuated vaccine, an alum-precipitated cell-free filtrate vaccine, and a recombinant protein vaccine. The purpose of this study was to assess the effectiveness, immunogenicity, and safety of these vaccines in preventing anthrax. To gather relevant data, a comprehensive search was conducted across multiple databases, including the Cochrane Infectious Diseases Group Specialized Register, CENTRAL, MEDLINE, EMBASE, LILACS, and mRCT, as of November 2008. Additionally, reference lists were reviewed to identify further studies. The inclusion criteria for this analysis were randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cluster-RCTs that compared anthrax vaccines with placebo, other non-anthrax vaccines, or no intervention. Studies comparing different administration routes or treatment regimens of anthrax vaccines were also included. Two independent reviewers assessed the eligibility of trials, evaluated the risk of bias, and extracted data. The primary outcomes analyzed were the incidence of anthrax cases and seroconversion rates, which were expressed as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Immunoglobulin G (IgG) concentrations were summarized using geometric means. A sensitivity analysis was performed to account for clustering effects in one cluster-RCT. However, no meta-analysis was conducted due to the nature of the data. The analysis included one cluster-RCT with 157,259 participants and four individual RCTs involving 1,917 participants. The cluster-RCT, conducted in the former USSR, demonstrated that a live-attenuated vaccine (referred to as STI) provided protection against clinical anthrax when compared to no vaccination. This protection was observed regardless of whether the vaccine was administered using a needleless device (RR 0.16; 102,737 participants, 154 clusters) or via the scarification method (RR 0.25; 104,496 participants, 151 clusters). While the confidence intervals were statistically significant in unadjusted analyses, the significance diminished when accounting for minor clustering effects. The four individual RCTs evaluated inactivated anthrax vaccines, including the anthrax vaccine absorbed (AVA) and recombinant protective antigen (rPA) vaccines. These studies revealed a dose-response relationship, with higher doses leading to increased anti-protective antigen IgG antibody titers. Intramuscular administration of the vaccine was associated with fewer injection site reactions compared to subcutaneous administration. Additionally, extending the interval between doses resulted in a lower frequency of injection site reactions. In conclusion, the evidence from one cluster-RCT suggests that live-attenuated anthrax vaccines may be effective in preventing cutaneous anthrax. Vaccines based on anthrax antigens were found to be immunogenic in most recipients, with minimal adverse events or reactions reported. Ongoing randomized controlled trials are continuing to evaluate the immunogenicity and safety profiles of anthrax vaccines.
